strengths: Well-motivated problem with concrete failure case (Django example) clearly illustrating the limitation of memoryless agents
Solid empirical improvements on two benchmarks (4.9% on SWE-bench-verified, 3.1% on SWE-bench-live) with consistent gains across ablations

Thorough experimental analysis including behavior shift analysis, nuanced cost-effectiveness evaluation, and per-repository breakdown revealing the relationship between commit history availability and performance gains
Practical, modular design that integrates easily into existing frameworks without fundamental changes
Excellent presentation with clear figures, comprehensive tool documentation, and well-structured narrative
Insightful finding that sparse retrieval (BM25) outperforms dense methods for code, with clear explanation rooted in code semantics
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily an engineering contribution applying existing techniques (BM25, LLM summarization) without introducing new concepts or methods

Critical practical limitation inadequately addressed: severe performance degradation with sparse commit history (67.4% → 54.3%, -13.1% on repositories with <10K commits) severely restricts applicability to many real-world projects
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices (7,000 commits, top-200 files) without ablation studies or sensitivity analysis to justify selections
LLM-generated summaries not evaluated: no quality metrics, human evaluation, or analysis of how summary inaccuracy affects localization
Limited evaluation scope: only file-level localization task (not end-to-end bug fixing), single framework integration (LocAgent), and small SWE-bench-live subset (130 examples)
Data leakage prevention underspecified: filtering criteria ('overlapping text') are vague and algorithmic details lacking
Error analysis insufficient: described as 'small-scale' without systematic characterization of when memory helps vs. hurts beyond citing novelty and retrieval failures
Cost overhead not fully addressed: average API cost increases but no clear heuristic for practitioners to decide when memory investment is worthwhile
Reproducibility concerns: GPT-4o dependency, no code release mentioned, repository-specific memory construction may not generalize
No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or cross-repository generalization studies

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clear articulation of memory limitation in agents, effectively illustrated through Django migration failure case (Figure 2)
Solid experimental results: Consistent improvements on both SWE-bench-verified (76.5% vs 71.6%, +4.9%) and SWE-bench-live (66.2% vs 63.1%), with positive ablations showing both components contribute

Thoughtful empirical analysis: Comprehensive investigation including behavior shift analysis (Figure 3), cost-effectiveness breakdown (Table 3), retrieval method comparison (Table 4), per-repository performance breakdown (Table 2), and honest error analysis

Practical design with good integration: Modular memory mechanisms integrate cleanly with LocAgent without major framework modifications; two complementary memory types (episodic + semantic) sensibly designed
Strong reproducibility: Detailed implementation documentation (§4.1), comprehensive appendices with tool examples and prompts, and promise of code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Memory mechanisms are straightforward (BM25 retrieval, frequency-based file selection), closely mirroring JiT-SDP literature; adding tools to agentic frameworks is incremental rather than novel

Fundamental dependency on repository history: Performance degrades significantly on sparse-history repos (Table 2: 54.3% vs 67.4%), with no principled mechanism to detect novelty or fall back; approach inapplicable to novel bugs unrelated to past commits

Semantic memory construction concerns: Frequency-based file selection is simplistic; circular evaluation (LocAgent generates summaries, then LocAgent+memory evaluated); only 83.1% coverage of target files in top-200 active (Table 5); no analysis of summary quality or hallucinations

Limited evaluation scope: Only tested on LocAgent (unclear generalization to Agentless or other frameworks); SWE-bench-live subset small (130 examples); all Python projects; file-level only; sensitivity analysis limited to Django repo

Retrieval quality inadequately validated: Relies on imperfect explicit commit-issue links; BM25 can retrieve distracting irrelevant commits (acknowledged via Figure 4 high variance); error analysis small-scale (§4.3); no systematic study of when memory hurts

Experimental design limitations: Fixed hyperparameters (K=200, 7000 commits) applied uniformly despite known variability; no comparison of alternative memory strategies (time-decay, developer experience, co-change patterns); no statistical significance testing; no analysis of scaling with repo size/age

Non-negligible cost overhead: Average cost increases 11-50% (Table 3), especially for failing cases; while justified on difficult problems, overall cost-benefit tradeoff and guidance for practical use underexplored

Generalization concerns: Evaluation limited to mature, open-source Python projects with rich histories; applicability to private codebases, other languages, young/new repositories, or cross-repository scenarios unclear or likely limited
